searchText: hmm that's not necessarily clear; we definitely want more storage use in periods where demand is higher, at least to some extent Why would we want that? State growth is effectively the same whether it happens Wednesday at noon or Sunday at midnight. Right, but the optimal amount of state is not the same when the demand is 10x higher I believe what we care about is the overall rate of growth, not *when* that growth occurs. Right, which is why I think we should separate out state storage costs. Yeah sorry by "when" I'm referring to the dimension that separates everett branches, not time 🤣 The 1559 technique gives us a way to do that without burdening the user with complexities in transaction pricing. Of course you were... 😛 the 1559 technique as is does effectively enforce the rule that the optimal amount of usage over anything more than the very short term is the same regardless of what the demand curve is hmm ok I guess now that I think about it, we can handle more volatility in state growth So perhaps state growth *should* be priced separately Historically, I believe the reason we have had a single gas pricing mechanism for *all* costs because the UX for users gets exponentially worse the the more knobs you give users. However, I think we can have a *fully automated* pricing mechanism for state growth that is *separate* from the pricing of network/CPU. yeah I see the rationale for this there's definitely value in a more stable max state size ceiling; it would guarantee that it all fits in ram for example State costs would be 100% burn, no "tip" for state growth because I think miners don't actually care about state growth, they care about block propagation time (network/cpu/storage access speed). The one challenge with going 2D is that it would make subcalls harder Why? Unless you still use "gas" as the primary metering resource, and just adjust gas costs And we could have the adjustment speed be really slow, like it doubles/halves daily or something (instead of every 6 blocks). It would use a separate metering system, but it would be paid for under the `max_fee` umbrella of 1559. ``` assert max_fee >= new_state_writes * block_state_fee + gas_used * (block_base_fee + inclusion_fee) ``` but if it uses a separate metering system, how would you restrict resource usage of subcalls? Would you update the CALL opcode to give both a gas and a storage-slots parameter? Don't we want to get rid of gas visibility? maybe There definitely have been use cases that have given me pause Optimistic rollup fraud proof execution, to give a random one Hmm, I think I see the problem. The problem is that the user sets a gas limit, not a total fee limit. I think total fee limit would more accurately represent user preference, and would make what I had in mind work (I think). But to be complete you'd need subcalls to be able to set total fee limits Only if we want to retain "gas visibility". right Personally, I think all calls should always forward all gas and it was a mistake (in hindsight) to allow limited gas passage to subcalls. And I do now think that if we want to get rid of it, we need to solve the problems of a bunch of use cases that rely on it Including optimism Why does optimism want it? Executing a fraud proof involves executing L2-transactions, which are inherently untrusted calls Why do they need to execute something *after* the fraud proof? That is, why isn't the fraud proof a tail call? well first of all, there may be multiple L2 transactions and you need to execute the N-1 remaining ones after the first But second, you need to actually process the block reverting after success Hmm, I thought the whole idea of rollups was that you *don't* need to execute multiple transactions? Rollups become 3x more inefficient if you have to provide a state root after every tx You only need to provide the state root between transactions during a proof game. Optimism's proof game is one-round Deliberate design choice for simplicity and to achieve stronger light client properties Ah, I see. That feels... not ideal... because it means your batch sizes are limited to the size of what can fit in a block, and it means fraud proofs can be *extremely* expensive on layer 1. (to the point where it may not be profitable to submit a fraud proof during times of L1 congestion) meh, fraud proofs are an exceptional case, and the overhead of 32 on-chain bytes per 5 million execution gas is very tolerable with the EIP 1559 basefee opcode you can just set the reward based on the fee level! That assumes the fraud proof comes in near the bond payment? 1. Attacker puts up bond just prior to congestion increase. 2. Fraud prover doesn't submit fraud proof because the bond is lower than gas cost to prove the fraud. Oh the bond requirements are definitely going to be high Even an eth2 validator-sized bond is more than sufficient even if gas prices go up to thousands of gwei Barely. 😬 The bond *has to* be high, because they are relying on the sequencer to provide cryptoeconomic pre-confirmations anyway 1000 nanoeth * 12.5M gas = 12.5 ETH That is in the same order of magnitude as validator bonds. And if L2 blocks can be as big as L1 blocks and there isn't a mechanism to narrow (like Arbitrum's multi-round bisection game), you may need to buy a whole block. My recollection is that they're going for fraud proof sizes somewhere in the 5-10M range Ah actually nvm, it's split across multiple transactions, so ok, 12.5M is more likely Depending on the bond size, it can work. If your bond is 100 ETH for example then it'll probably be fine. I don't see why it can't be 100 ETH! Sequencing is a specialized activity, and they need high bonds anyway to make the cryptoeconomic pre-confirmations meaningful Circling back, the worry here is that someone will construct a transaction that causes OOG on L1? yeah, the worry is that the sequencer makes a batch with a fraudulent state root, and this batch's first transaction causes an OOG on L1 so the fraud proof can never be fully submitted Any batch that fails on L1 is considered fraudulent? hmm I have no idea it could be that a transaction that OOGs if executed is a no-op btw you may want to just talk to Karl or Ben directly 🤣 So they specifically want to limit gas to sub-transactions, not to have a well defined amount of gas remaining at the end? hmm not sure, need to ask them `call { gasRemainingAfter: xxx }()` would be a potential option otherwise. That way we remove observability, but retain the ability to effectively have try/finally blocks. there's definitely clever alternatives, another one I had is that the user access list includes a list of how much gas is allotted to each address So the gas allocation is all done outside the EVM We would need first class sub-transactions though wouldn't we? why? Oh, you mean each address in the call tree gets a fixed amount of gas? No, I mean an access list would be of the form {ADDR1: 100000, ADDR2: 870000, ADD3: 50000} Would you define the whole tree? What if one contract is called twice in the tree (in two different branches)? The current call context would take gas from the pool that is closest in the call stack So if the contract is called twice those two calls would just share gas What if Bob has two transactions in a batch? And if you don't like that, you'd have to route the two calls through two separate forwarder contracts Those gas allowances would need to be available to the EVM I think for the fraud proofs to verify that enough gas was provided. true well technically you could make the fraud proof 2 txs and require the second to contain a merkle proof of the first lol Merkle Proofs: The hammer to all of Ethereum's nails. 🤣 there's a reason Charles H tried so hard to make Ralph Merkle an official EF advisor way back in those good old days
